Andrew Oates reported that some macOS hosts could repeatedly
send FIN packets even if the remote peer drops them and
send back DUP ACK RWIN 0 packets.
<quoting Andrew>
20:27:16.968254 gif0  In  IP macos > victim: Flags [SEW]
20:27:16.968339 gif0  Out IP victim > macos: Flags [S.E]
20:27:16.968833 gif0  In  IP macos > victim: Flags [.]
20:27:16.968885 gif0  In  IP macos > victim: Flags [P.]
20:27:16.968896 gif0  Out IP victim > macos: Flags [.]
20:27:19.454593 gif0  In  IP macos > victim: Flags [F.]
20:27:19.454675 gif0  Out IP victim > macos: Flags [.]
20:27:19.455116 gif0  In  IP macos > victim: Flags [F.]
The retransmits/dup-ACKs then repeat in a tight loop.
</quoting Andrew>
RFC 9293 3.4. Sequence Numbers states :
Note that when the receive window is zero no segments should be
acceptable except ACK segments.  Thus
column2: it is be possible for a TCP to

column1: maintain a zero receive window while transmitting data and receiving
ACKs.  However
column2: even when the receive window is zero

column1: process the RST and URG fields of all incoming segments.
Even if we could consider a bare FIN.ACK packet to be an ACK in RFC terms
the retransmits should use exponential backoff.
Accepting the FIN in linux does not add extra memory costs
because the FIN flag will simply be merged to the tail skb in
the receive queue
